meanings.English: To be, to become, to exist, to happen
meanings.Hindi: hona, vidyaman hona, utpann hona, ghatit hona

pedagogy.concept: The root BU primarily means 'to be' or 'to become' in the active voice (parasmaipada). However, when taking specific suffixes, prefixes, or entering the passive or impersonal (bhāva) constructions, its sense can shift to denote states of mutual action, inherent qualities, or impersonal occurrences.

Depending on the specific sense and usage, it shifts between intransitive and transitive behaviours, and can form standard desiderative (sananta) and causative (ṇijanta) derivatives.

meanings.English: To be satisfied, to rejoice, to be pleased
meanings.Hindi: santusht hona, prasanna hona, trupt hona
meanings.Bengali: tripto হওয়া, santushto হওয়া, anondito হওয়া
meanings.German: zufrieden sein, sich freuen, satt werden
meanings.French: etre satisfait, se rejouir, etre content
meanings.Chinese: man yi, gao xing, xi yue

pedagogy.concept: The root tfp (tṛp) primarily expresses the state of being satisfied or pleased. Since this root belongs to the fourth gaṇa and takes ātmanepada endings in its basic intransitive sense, it highlights an internal feeling of contentment or fulfillment experienced by the subject.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), third-person singular, ātmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The child is satisfied with the food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causal base (ṇic) with parasmaipada endings
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone else to be pleased or satisfied, to satiate

meanings.English: To rejoice, to be infatuated, to be bewildered, to become arrogant
meanings.Kannada: santosha padu, moha kolļu, bhrānti hondu, garvisu
meanings.Hindi: prasanna hona, mohit hona, bhramit hona, ahankar karna
meanings.Bengali: ananda paoya, mohita haoya, bhranta haoya, garba kara
meanings.German: sich freuen, betört sein, verwirrt sein, stolz sein
meanings.French: se réjouir, être infatué, être égaré, devenir arrogant

pedagogy.concept: The root dfpa belongs to the fourth gaṇa and takes ātmanepada endings. Its core meaning encompasses both exhilaration or joy (harṣa) and mental delusion, infatuation, or arrogance (moha).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative passive or standard passive form indicating the action of causing delusion or arrogance.
scenarios.meaning: To be made arrogant or to be driven into delusion.
scenarios.example_english: He is made arrogant by bad counsel.

meanings.English: To seek to harm, to bear malice, to plot against, to injure
meanings.Hindi: droha karna, hanikaran karna, bura sochna
meanings.Bengali: droh kara, apakar kara, kshati kara
meanings.French: vouloir du mal, nuire, être hostile
meanings.Chinese: huai yi, jia hai, yuan hen

pedagogy.concept: The root druha means to seek to harm or bear malice towards someone. In grammar, the person who is the object of this hostility typically takes the dative case.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, 3rd person singular, atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: He seeks to harm or bears malice
scenarios.example_english: He bears malice towards the virtuous person.

meanings.English: To be bewildered, to lose consciousness, to be confused, to err
meanings.Hindi: bramhit hona, mohit hona, behosh hona, bhulna
meanings.Bengali: mohito hao, bhrom howa, abodh howa, ajnan
meanings.German: verwirrt sein, irregehen, den Verstand verlieren, sich irren
meanings.French: etre egaré, etre confus, perdre la raison

pedagogy.concept: The root muh signifies mental bewilderment, confusion, or loss of presence of mind. In its causative form, it extends to actively confusing or deluding someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root to indicate causing another to experience the action.
scenarios.meaning: To delude or confuse someone else.

meanings.English: To vomit, to spew, to eject

pedagogy.concept: The root zRuha~ primarily means to vomit or spew out. In its causative form, it shifts from the basic physical action of ejection to causing someone or something else to spew or emit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to vomit or to make someone spew out
scenarios.example_english: The doctor causes the patient to vomit with the medicine.

meanings.English: To love, to feel affection, to be fond of
meanings.Kannada: priti madu, sneha iru, nentu koḷḷu
meanings.Tamil: anbu kol, nesam iru, paṭru vai
meanings.Hindi: prem karna, sneh rakhna, anurag hona

pedagogy.concept: The root zRiha (to feel affection or love) primarily takes Atmanepada endings to express internal emotional states or personal attachment. When modified into causative or derivative forms, it shifts toward inducing that affection in others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Passive voice or intransitive emotional state in Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: To be loved or to experience affection naturally.
scenarios.example_english: The child feels affection toward the mother.

meanings.English: To become calm, to be pacified, to be quiet
meanings.Bengali: shanta হওয়া, thanda হওয়া, nibe jaoya

pedagogy.concept: The root sam (Samu~) primarily conveys the sense of pacification, subsiding, or becoming calm. When modified into the causative form, it shifts from an intransitive state of calming down to the transitive action of causing something or someone else to become pacified or quiet.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root to express making someone or something else calm.
scenarios.meaning: To pacify, to cause to subside, to quench

meanings.English: To desire, to long for, to wish, to yearn

pedagogy.concept: The root tamu~ primarily expresses yearning or strong desire. When modified into causative or desiderative forms, the nuance shifts to causing that longing or desiring intensely for oneself.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, fourth conjugation parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: To desire or to be afflicted/exhausted by longing
scenarios.example_english: The devotee longs for the Lord.

meanings.English: To tame, to subdue, to be quiet, to control oneself
meanings.Hindi: Shant hona, vash mein karna, daman karna
meanings.Bengali: Damon kora, shanto howa, bash e ana

pedagogy.concept: The root damu implies calming, subduing, or taming. When used in its basic form, it conveys the taming of senses or creatures, while the causative form shifts the action to actively causing someone or something to become subdued or disciplined.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), 3rd person singular, parasmaipada of divādi-gaṇa
scenarios.meaning: He becomes tame, controls himself, or subdues.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) present tense, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: He tames or causes someone to be subdued.

meanings.English: To be weary, to tire, to exert oneself, to suffer

pedagogy.concept: The root Sramu means to exert oneself or to feel fatigue and undergo austerity. Through morphological additions like the causative suffix, the sense shifts from simply feeling tired oneself to causing someone else to exert effort or undergo penance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative marker nic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to toil or undergo austerity
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the disciple undergo austerity through penance.

meanings.English: To wander, to roam, to err, to waver

pedagogy.concept: The root Bramu~ conveys the sense of unsteadiness, wandering, or mental confusion. In its causative form, it shifts from expressing the subject's own wandering or delusion to actively causing someone else to wander or be confused.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root with guṇa
scenarios.meaning: To cause to wander, to delude or mislead someone
scenarios.example_english: Illusion causes all people to wander (deludes all people).

meanings.English: To endure, to tolerate, to forgive, to be patient
meanings.Hindi: Sahan karna, kshama karna, bardasht karna

pedagogy.concept: The root kṣam means to endure or forgive. When used in different forms like the causative or with upasargas, the nuance shifts from simply bearing something passively to actively pardoning someone or making oneself capable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: To cause to forgive, to ask for forgiveness
scenarios.example_english: The devotee asks God for forgiveness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: With upasarga ā
scenarios.meaning: To challenge, to be jealous or impatient
scenarios.example_english: The enemy does not tolerate the friend.

meanings.English: To grow tired, to become exhausted, to languish, to droop
meanings.Hindi: thaknā, mlan honā, thak kar chur honā, murjhānā
meanings.Bengali: klānta haoẏā, mlān haoẏā, jhiye paṛā

pedagogy.concept: The root klamu~ expresses physical or mental weariness and fading energy. When used in its basic form, it denotes getting tired naturally, whereas in the causative form, it signifies tiring someone else out or causing exhaustion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), 3rd person singular, active voice (parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: Walking on the path, he gets tired.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) stem in present tense, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to grow tired or exhausts them
scenarios.example_english: The long question exhausts the child.

meanings.English: To rejoice, to be intoxicated, to languish, to tire
meanings.Hindi: Khushi hona, harshit hona, thak jana

pedagogy.concept: The root madI expresses a duality of experience: the soaring height of joy or exhilaration, and the downward pull of weariness or languishing. When used in its causative or derived forms, this emotional and physical intensity often shifts towards causing delight or becoming intoxicated.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To gladden, to cause to rejoice or intoxicate

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl

pedagogy.concept: The root asu~ primarily means throwing or casting. When prefixes are added, the direction or specific nature of the throwing changes, and causative forms emphasize the act of causing something to be thrown.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the upasarga sam- to indicate bringing together or throwing into a unified collection.
scenarios.meaning: To combine, to compound, to synthesize
scenarios.example_english: The grammarian compounds the words together.

meanings.English: To strive, to attempt, to exert oneself
meanings.Hindi: prayatna karna, koshish karna, sram karna
meanings.Bengali: cheshta kara, prayatna kara, shram kara

pedagogy.concept: The root yasu~ primarily denotes effort or striving. When modified into causative or other derived forms, the sense shifts to causing someone else to exert themselves or striving intensely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present, parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He strives or makes an effort
scenarios.example_english: He strives earnestly for the work.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative with ṇic
scenarios.meaning: He causes to strive or urges
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to strive for the work.

meanings.English: To release, to set free, to abandon, to let go
meanings.Chinese: shi fang, jie tuo, fang qi

pedagogy.concept: The root jasu conveys the core sense of releasing, liberating, or letting go of something. Through various suffixes and prefixes, this action can be directed towards freeing bound entities or discarding objects entirely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to release or to set someone else free
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the bound thief to be released.

meanings.English: To diminish, to decay, to waste away, to exhaust

pedagogy.concept: The root tasu means to diminish or decay. When modified into the causative form, it conveys the active action of causing something to diminish or exhaust.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple future tense, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The body will waste away with time.

meanings.English: To waste away, to decay, to diminish, to perish
meanings.Chinese: xiao hao, jian shao, shuai tui

pedagogy.concept: The root dasu (upakshaye) primarily expresses the gradual loss, decay, or exhaustion of something. When shifted into the causative form, it describes the active destruction or depletion of an object by an agent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to cause an action, turning the intransitive sense of wasting away into a transitive action of causing destruction or depletion.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to diminish, to waste away, to deplete something actively
scenarios.example_english: He causes the wealth to waste away.

meanings.English: To stop, to make firm, to support, to stay

pedagogy.concept: The root vasu means to make firm or stop. When used in causative or prefixed forms, it often extends to supporting or holding something firmly in place.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root to denote making someone stop or support.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to stop or to support
scenarios.example_english: The tree supports the ground firmly.

meanings.English: To stop, to make firm, to pillar, to stay

pedagogy.concept: The root basu means to make firm or to stop and pillar. It can take causative forms to express the action of causing something to become stiff or stationary.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem basayati
scenarios.meaning: To cause to stop or to render stiff
scenarios.example_english: He causes the fast horse to stop.

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute

pedagogy.concept: The root yusa~ primarily expresses the action of dividing, separating, or apportioning. In its causative form, it conveys the active agency of causing something to be divided or distributed among recipients.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to the root, changing its valence to make someone cause a division.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or to distribute
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the books to be distributed.

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute

pedagogy.concept: The root vyuz represents the action of division or separation. Through various suffixes and prefixes, it can indicate the state of being divided or the active process of separating components.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Application of the prefix vi- denoting thorough separation in the present tense

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute
meanings.Bengali: bhāga karā, bāṭoyārā karā, pr̥thaka karā

pedagogy.concept: The root vyusa implies division or separation, and through causative forms, it actively expresses the action of causing something to be divided or distributed among recipients.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) suffix added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or to distribute
scenarios.example_english: He causes the fruit to be divided.

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute

pedagogy.concept: The root byusa expresses the action of dividing, separating, or distributing. Its basic meaning shifts depending on prefixes or grammatical formations to indicate specific kinds of separation or distribution.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Application of the prefix vi- to emphasize complete separation or division.
scenarios.meaning: To distribute completely or divide into parts.

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to scatter

pedagogy.concept: The root busa~ primarily conveys the sense of division or separation. When used in causative or prefixed forms, it emphasizes the intentional act of scattering or partitioning objects.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to denote the causative action
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or to scatter about
scenarios.example_english: He causes the wood to be split or scattered.

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute
meanings.Bengali: bhāga karā, vibhakta karā, alāda karā

pedagogy.concept: The root vusa~ primarily conveys the action of dividing, separating, or distributing. When modified into various derived forms, the fundamental sense of division shifts to causing division or intensive separation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) of vusa~
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or to distribute
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the books to be distributed among the students.

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute

pedagogy.concept: The root pyuza~ primarily means to divide or distribute. When modified with prefixes or conjugated in specific derived forms, the action of division takes on nuanced directions such as separating parts or distributing among many.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of prefix vi- to the present indicative active form
scenarios.meaning: To divide thoroughly or distribute into parts

meanings.English: To divide, to separate, to distribute

pedagogy.concept: The root pyusa~ fundamentally conveys the action of dividing, separating, or distributing. Through various suffixes and prefixes, this basic sense of division can be directed towards objects or translated into causative actions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix -ṇic added to the root, inducing Guṇa.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or to distribute.
scenarios.example_english: He causes the goods to be distributed.

meanings.English: To divide, to split, to distribute, to separate
meanings.Hindi: bāṇṭnā, vibhajit karnā, alag karnā, ṭukḍā karnā
meanings.Bengali: bhāg karā, vibhakta karā, alāda karā, tuṇḍa karā

pedagogy.concept: The root puza~ carries the core sense of division or distribution. When modified into causative or prefixed forms, it shifts from the act of dividing an object oneself to causing a distribution or separation among multiple agents.

scenarios.form: causative (pohayati / poṣayati - causative stem, noting root vowel changes)
scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to express the causative meaning of causing someone else to divide or distribute.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to divide or distribute
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the disciples to distribute the wealth.

meanings.English: To burn, to scorch, to inflame

pedagogy.concept: The root pluza~ primarily means to burn or scorch. In its causative form, it expresses the action of causing something to burn or setting fire to an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the nic suffix to form the causative stem, indicating the instigation of burning.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to burn, to set on fire

meanings.English: To urge, to send, to impel, to direct

pedagogy.concept: The root visa~ generally means to urge, send, or impel. By applying causative morphology, the sense shifts towards actively causing another to send or direct something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the causative suffix -aya to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to send or to instigate
scenarios.example_english: The teacher directs the student to send.

meanings.English: To urge, to impel, to incite, to send
meanings.Chinese: tui dong, pai chu, ji fa

pedagogy.concept: The root bisa~ fundamentally means to impel, urge, or send. When morphological shifts like the causal or desiderative are applied, the sense of compelling an action or desiring to prompt someone becomes prominent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causal base formation (nic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: To cause to urge, to cause to send or prompt someone
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the pupil to be urged toward the task.

meanings.English: To bind, to connect, to embrace, to join

pedagogy.concept: The root kusa~ primarily expresses the action of binding, joining, or bringing things together in close contact. In its derived forms, this sense of connection can be directed reflexively or intensified through causative suffixes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the ṇic suffix to cause someone else to bind or connect.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to bind or to assemble together.
scenarios.example_english: The garland-maker causes the flowers to be strung together.

meanings.English: To embrace, to clasp, to unite, to hold

pedagogy.concept: The root kuSa means to embrace, cling, or unite. When modified with prefixes or used in causative forms, the action of embracing or binding extends from physical contact to metaphorical holding and gathering.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the prefix sam-
scenarios.meaning: To embrace completely, to press together tightly, to synthesize
scenarios.example_english: The creeper embraces the tree completely.

meanings.English: To sweat, to perspire, to ooze

pedagogy.concept: The root YizvidA~ primarily describes physical moisture excretion or sweating from the body. Through causative formation, it can be extended to mean causing something to sweat or excrete fluid.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative marker nic added to the root to denote making someone or something sweat.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to sweat, to make perspire
scenarios.example_english: The sun makes the man sweat with its heat.

meanings.English: To endure, to tolerate, to forgive, to be patient
meanings.Hindi: Sahan karna, kshama karna, bardasht karna

pedagogy.concept: The root kzam expresses enduring or forgiving. By adding causative suffixes, the meaning shifts to making someone tolerate or asking for forgiveness, and nominal forms highlight patience as an intrinsic quality.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the causative suffix 'nic' to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to endure or to make someone pardon
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student apologize.

meanings.English: (uncertain)

pedagogy.concept: This root indicates the act of abandoning, discharging, or emitting. Because it is relatively rare and lacks widely attested derived-form nuances that are standardly taught, no specific secondary scenarios are listed.

meanings.English: To crush, to break, to destroy, to fragment

pedagogy.concept: The root musa~ fundamentally means to break or to fragment. Through various derivative forms, this sense of destruction or breaking can be directed towards causing someone else to break something or intensifying the act.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to break or to shatter something
scenarios.example_english: He causes the enemy to be crushed.

meanings.English: To ripen, to mature, to result, to transform

pedagogy.concept: The root masI~ primarily conveys the sense of ripening, maturing, or resulting in a final state of transformation. When modified by prefixes or turned into causative forms, it highlights the process or agency of bringing something to completion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) affix added to express the act of causing to mature or ripen.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to ripen, to cook, to bring to maturity.

meanings.English: To ripen, to mature, to cook fully, to result

pedagogy.concept: The root samI~ (class 4 parasmaipada) primarily denotes ripening, maturing, or bringing something to its ultimate completion and result. In derived forms like the causative, it expresses the active process of cooking, ripening, or maturing an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the ṇic suffix to the root to indicate an agent causing the ripening or cooking action.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to ripen, to cook, to bring to completion

meanings.English: To stir, to agitate, to churn, to toss about

pedagogy.concept: The root luwa~ carries the primary sense of stirring, agitating, or churning. When used in causative forms, it emphasizes the action of causing a liquid or mass to be thoroughly stirred or mixed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix nic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to stir or agitate intensely

meanings.English: To roll, to toss about, to agitate

pedagogy.concept: The root luWa~ (to roll or agitate) primarily expresses rolling or tossing about. When modified into the causative form, it signifies causing an object to roll or turn over.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to roll or to churn

meanings.English: To assemble, to collect, to gather, to unite
meanings.Bengali: ektrito kora, jama kora, milito howa
meanings.Chinese: ju ji, ji he, hui he

pedagogy.concept: The root uca~ fundamentally expresses the coming together or assembly of things. When used with various prepositions, this sense of gathering or combining can be directed towards mental adaptation or physical accumulation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ta suffix forming a past passive participle indicating suitability or proper assembly
scenarios.example_english: This conduct was proper for all.

meanings.English: To fall down, to drop, to sink, to collapse
meanings.Bengali: Niche pora, khose pora, bhonge pora

pedagogy.concept: The root BfSu denotes falling downwards. In its basic active form (parasmaipada), it describes the direct physical action of falling or dropping. Through causative suffixes, it expresses the act of causing someone or something to fall down.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem, making it transitive.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to fall, to drop down
scenarios.example_english: He causes the fruit to fall from the tree.

meanings.English: To become wet, to be moist, to become damp

pedagogy.concept: The root stima~ expresses the physical state of becoming moist or wet. In its causative form, it conveys the active agency of moistening or wetting an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) formation indicating action done to another

meanings.English: To fall down, to slip, to drop

pedagogy.concept: The root BranSu~ expresses the physical action of falling or slipping downwards. In causative forms, it conveys the action of causing something or someone to fall.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic) suffix added to the root to indicate active causation
scenarios.meaning: To cause to fall, to drop
scenarios.example_english: He causes the fruit to fall from the tree.

meanings.English: To cover, to veil, to enclose, to conceal

pedagogy.concept: The root vfSa~ primarily expresses the action of covering or enclosing. By adding various affixes, such as causative morphemes or prefixes, the sense extends from literal physical covering to metaphorically concealing or protecting.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to the root to indicate causing someone to cover or cause to conceal.
scenarios.meaning: To cause to cover or to cause to conceal.
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to be covered with a cloth.

meanings.English: To make thin, to waste away, to weaken, to emaciate
meanings.Hindi: patla hona, durbal hona, kshinhona, sukna
meanings.Bengali: choto hoa, patla hoa, kshin hoa, durbal hoa

pedagogy.concept: The root kfSa means to become thin or to make thin. When used in its causative form, the action shifts from a natural state of wasting away to actively causing something to become lean or emaciated.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix णिच् (nic) added to the base root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to become thin or to emaciate

meanings.English: To thirst, to be thirsty, to desire
meanings.Bengali: trishna paoya, piyaas laaga, ichchha kara

pedagogy.concept: The root YitfzA~ primarily expresses the physical state of thirst or, by extension, an intense craving and desire. In its causative form, it signifies causing someone or something to thirst or desire.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), 3rd person singular, parasmaipada
Causative (ṇic), present tense (laṭ), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to thirst or makes desirous
scenarios.example_english: The hot sunshine makes the whole world thirst.

meanings.English: To rejoice, to thrill, to be glad, to bristle
meanings.Kannada: santosha padu, romanchana gondu, pulakita gondu
meanings.Hindi: prasanna hona, romanchit hona, khush hona
meanings.Bengali: anandita হওয়া, pulakita হওয়া, khushi হওয়া

pedagogy.concept: The root hfza~ primarily denotes joy, exhilaration, or the physical bristling of hair associated with intense emotion. When modified into the causative form, it expresses the action of causing someone else to experience this joy or excitement.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to rejoice or thrill
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes him rejoice with the news of the son.

meanings.English: To injure, to harm, to hurt
meanings.Hindi: hinsa karna, nuksan pahunchana, chot dena
meanings.Bengali: hingsa kora, akromon kora, chot deoa
meanings.Chinese: 伤害, 侵害, 打伤

pedagogy.concept: The root ruza carries the core sense of causing injury or doing harm. Through causative derivations, it extends to the deliberate act of causing someone else to injure or provoke.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nijanta) suffix ṇic added to the base root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to injure or to provoke anger
scenarios.example_english: He causes the enemy to be injured.

meanings.English: To injure, to harm, to hurt

meanings.Bengali: andho kara, drishti noshto kara, andhokar kora
meanings.French: aveugler, obscurcir la vue, priver de la vue
meanings.Chinese: shi mang, zhezhu shixian, qingchu shili

pedagogy.concept: The root anDa belongs to the cur-ādi gaṇa (class 10) and primarily conveys the sense of causing blindness or impairing vision. Through causative formations and derived nominals, it describes both physical blinding and metaphorical obscuration of clarity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laT) active voice of the cur-ādi gaṇa root.
scenarios.meaning: To blind or to obscure vision.
scenarios.example_english: He blinds the enemy with brilliance.

meanings.English: To punish, to fine, to chastise, to penalize
meanings.Hindi: Dand dena, saja dena, dandan karna

pedagogy.concept: The root danqa primarily means to punish or levy a fine. When modified into the causative or passive forms, it shifts the focus onto the agent causing the punishment or the subject undergoing the penalty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the nic suffix to engage another person in the act of punishing.
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to punish or to order a punishment
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the thief to be punished.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Changing the verb voice to passive, making the recipient of the punishment the grammatical subject.
scenarios.meaning: To be punished or to suffer a fine
scenarios.example_english: The thief is punished by the king.

meanings.English: To mark, to brand, to characterize, to trace
meanings.Hindi: chinhit karna, lakshan dena, ankit karna
meanings.Bengali: chihniyta kora, lakshan deoa, ankito kora
meanings.Chinese: biao ji, biao shi, hua zhi

pedagogy.concept: The root anka in the tenth conjugation expresses the action of marking, stamping, or setting a characteristic sign. In its standard causative or derived verbal forms, it often emphasizes the act of stamping an emblem or clearly distinguishing something through a visible sign.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third person singular, parasmaipada of the tenth conjugation curadigana
scenarios.meaning: He marks, he brands, or he sets a sign upon something.

meanings.English: To mark, to characterize, to indicate

pedagogy.concept: The root anga in the tenth conjugation expresses the action of marking, designating, or indicating a characteristic. Through derivation into the causative or other forms, its basic notion of marking or pointing out can be directed towards objects or actions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present indicative active, 3rd person singular in the tenth conjugation

meanings.English: To make happy, to give pleasure, to delight
meanings.Hindi: khush karna, anand dena, prasanna karna
meanings.French: rendre heureux, réjouir, donner du plaisir
meanings.Chinese: shi kuai le, zhu fu, shi man yi

pedagogy.concept: The root suKa in the tenth gaṇa expresses the action of making someone happy or causing pleasure. Through grammatical derivations, it can shift to describe a state of experiencing that happiness or expressing delight.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Denominative suffix ya applied to the derived nominal base to indicate causing happiness
scenarios.meaning: To cause happiness or comfort to someone

meanings.English: (uncertain)

pedagogy.concept: This root relates to causing or experiencing distress or pain in the context of specific actions, but it has very limited productive usage and lacks standard comparative paradigms worth dividing into multiple scenarios.

meanings.English: To taste, to relish, to moisten, to lubricate
meanings.Kannada: Ruchi nodu, svadishtu padu, sneha madu, jneha
meanings.Hindi: Svad lena, ras chakhna, chikna karna
meanings.Bengali: Rasa nova, asvadana kara, snigdha kara

pedagogy.concept: The root rasa primarily means to taste or relish, and also to moisten or lubricate. Through causative and derivative formations, the sense shifts between experiencing a flavor or essence and imparting moisture or oiliness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix -aya added to the root
scenarios.meaning: To cause to taste or to flavor

meanings.English: To spend, to expend, to disburse, to waste
meanings.Chinese: hua fei, kai xiao, xiao hao

pedagogy.concept: The root vyaya belongs to the tenth conjugation and primarily expresses the act of spending or expending wealth. Through causative and nominal derivations, it can highlight the action of causing expense or the state of being diminished.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense active (parasmaipada) of the primitive root in class 10.

meanings.English: To shape, to form, to give form
meanings.Hindi: Rup dena, akriti banana, srijan karna
meanings.Bengali: Rup dewa, gathan kara, akriti dewa

pedagogy.concept: The root rUp in the tenth gaNa primarily denotes the action of shaping, forming, or giving visual manifestation to something. Through the causative-like inflection of the curAdi gaNa, it expresses the active process of crafting or fashioning an object into a specific shape.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present indicative (laT) third person singular in the tenth gaNa (curAdi)
scenarios.meaning: To shape, to form, or to give a definite appearance to an object

meanings.English: To divide, to split, to cut in two

pedagogy.concept: The root Ceda in the tenth gaṇa primarily expresses the action of dividing, cutting, or splitting something into two parts. In its causative and derived forms, the sense of active splitting or causing a division becomes more intensive.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: 10th gaṇa present tense third person singular
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter causes the wood to be cut.

meanings.English: To cover, to conceal, to hide

pedagogy.concept: The root cada carries the primary sense of covering or concealing. In the causative form, it often denotes the act of causing to cover or displaying a false appearance, mimicking or pretending.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem chadayati, meaning to cause to cover or to disguise.
scenarios.meaning: To disguise, to pretend, or to put on a false appearance.

meanings.English: To urge, to impel, to incite, to direct

pedagogy.concept: The root lABa in the tenth gaṇa carries the causative sense of urging or directing someone to action. Through the addition of verbal prefixes or nominal suffixes, the fundamental nuance of impelling shifts toward specific directions or goals.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the prefix pra- to the tenth gaṇa present stem
scenarios.meaning: To strongly urge or incite someone toward an action
scenarios.example_english: The teacher strongly urges the student toward a good deed

meanings.English: To crush limbs, to bruise, to wound, to grind
meanings.Telugu: gatra vicurnana, gayamu ceyu, picci ceyu
meanings.Hindi: ang vicurna karna, ghayal karna, kuchalna
meanings.Bengali: anga vicurna kara, ahata kara, curna kara

pedagogy.concept: The root vraRa primarily means to crush or bruise the body. Through the causative form, it describes the action of causing someone to bruise or injure another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to crush or to inflict a wound on another
scenarios.example_english: The army causes the enemy to be wounded.

meanings.English: To describe, to paint, to elaborate, to praise
meanings.Hindi: varnan karna, vyakhya karna, stuti karna
meanings.Bengali: varnana kara, byakhya kara, prashamsa kara

pedagogy.concept: The root varRa primarily conveys the act of describing, detailing, or attributing qualities to something. Through causative formations, it expresses the action of causing something to be described or depicted vividly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the root with the prefix vi
scenarios.meaning: To explain in detail or elaborate clearly
scenarios.example_english: The teacher explains the meaning of the text in detail.

meanings.English: To be green, to become green, to flourish

pedagogy.concept: The root parRa belongs to the tenth conjugation and primarily denotes the state of being green or flourishing. When used in causative or derivative forms, it shifts from merely describing a state of color to actively causing vegetation to become green.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense, third-person singular in the active voice (parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: In the spring, the earth turns green.

meanings.English: To see, to look, to observe, to perceive
meanings.Hindi: Dekhna, dekh bhal karna, avalokan karna

pedagogy.concept: The root vizka belongs to the tudadi or curadi classes in various contexts with the basic sense of seeing or observing. When used in different derived forms such as the causative, the sense shifts towards causing someone to see or display something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: curadi gaṇa present tense third person singular
scenarios.meaning: To show or to cause to see
scenarios.example_english: The teacher shows the picture to the student.

meanings.English: To throw, to cast, to hurl, to send

pedagogy.concept: The root kzip primarily means to throw or cast. When modified into the causative form, it emphasizes the action of impelling, inciting, or directing someone or something toward an action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Adding the ṇic suffix to form kṣipayati
scenarios.meaning: To cause to throw, to impel, or to urge on
scenarios.example_english: The master urges the servant to drive the horse.

meanings.English: To dwell, to reside, to inhabit, to live

pedagogy.concept: The root vasa in the tenth gaṇa generally expresses dwelling or inhabiting. With various prefixes, it can nuance the sense to entering a dwelling, lingering, or dwelling together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the prefix ni- to the root vasa in the present tense
scenarios.meaning: To dwell, to reside in a place

meanings.English: To cover, to conceal, to veil, to protect

pedagogy.concept: The root tutTa primarily means to cover or conceal. In its causative and derived nominal contexts, this sense shifts towards causing something to be covered or protected by an agent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the causative suffixaya
scenarios.meaning: To cause to cover or to have something concealed
scenarios.example_english: The protector causes the house to be covered.

meanings.English: To cut, to sow, to reap, to scatter

pedagogy.concept: The root palyUla primarily combines the physical actions of cutting or reaping with scattering or sowing seeds. In its causative and derived nominal forms, the focus shifts between the agricultural act of harvesting and the dispersal of materials.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), parasmaipada, third person singular
scenarios.example_english: The farmer sows the seed in the field.

meanings.English: To speak, to converse, to talk
meanings.Chinese: shuo hua, jiang hua, tan hua

pedagogy.concept: The root ruṭh carries the core sense of speaking or language use. When modified into causative or derivative forms, the emphasis shifts toward causing speech or engaging in specific conversational contexts.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative suffix ṇic added to the tenth conjugation root
scenarios.meaning: To cause someone to speak or to make articulate sounds
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student speak.

meanings.English: To see, to look at, to perceive

pedagogy.concept: The root Deka means to see or perceive. In its causative form, it typically indicates causing someone to see or showing something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Addition of the nic suffix to form the causative stem
scenarios.meaning: To cause to see, to show
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to see the book.
